# Access Right

`admin.obj.core.access_right` · v2.0.0 · **draft** · scope **core**

> A single, named permission held by a single, named identity, granted for a stated reason, in force until somebody removes it. The object is not the permission — permissions are defined once by whoever built the system and are the same for everyone. The object is the GRANT: who holds it, who authorised it, why, when it was last actually used, and when anybody last asked whether the reason still holds. Access is the only administrative asset that costs nothing to hold and accumulates by default, which is why an organisation's entitlement count only ever goes up and why the number nobody can produce on request is how many of them are still needed.


**The discriminator.** The grant REASON, not the permission. If nobody can say why this identity holds this entitlement, it is not an Access Right — it is a finding waiting for an auditor, because review means asking whether the reason still holds and a reviewer handed a list with no reasons has exactly two options: rubber-stamp everything, or break something. They pick the first, every time, which is why recertification campaigns approve upwards of ninety per cent of what they are shown and change almost nothing.


Also called: `Entitlement`, `Permission`, `Grant`, `Authorisation`, `Membership`, `Licence Seat`


### Questions this object answers

- Who can do this, in which system, and on whose authority?
- Why do they have it, and does that reason still exist?
- When was it last used — and has it ever been used at all?
- When was it last reviewed, by whom, and did the review actually look?
- If this identity turned hostile tomorrow, what exactly could it reach?


### What it is NOT responsible for

- NOT the identity or the account. The account is WHO; this is WHAT THEY MAY DO. One identity holds many access rights, and conflating them is why "we disabled his account" is offered as proof of revocation when the federated SaaS seats, the shared service credential he knew and the building pass in his drawer are all untouched.

- NOT a role. A role is a BUNDLE of entitlements maintained by somebody else. Roles are how access is granted efficiently and are the reason nobody can answer what an individual can actually do — the entitlement is the unit of risk, the role is the unit of convenience.

- NOT a policy. `admin.obj.core.policy` states the rule ("access is granted on least privilege, reviewed quarterly"). This object is one instance the rule is supposed to govern, and the gap between the two is the whole of access administration.

- NOT an approval. `admin.obj.core.approval` is the one-time decision that let the grant happen. This object is what that decision left behind and what outlives it, usually by years.

## Preconditions

- **`acr.reason_before_grant`** A testable business reason exists before the entitlement is created. _(unmet → Block the grant. This is the cheapest control in the whole domain and the one most often skipped: a reason costs thirty seconds at grant time and is unrecoverable afterwards, because the only people who knew it have moved on.
)_
- **`acr.named_individual_holder`** A named individual holds the entitlement, or the identity is explicitly registered as non-human with an owner. _(unmet → Route to the system owner. An entitlement with no accountable party cannot be reviewed or safely revoked.)_
- **`acr.approval_before_privileged_grant`** Privileged and administrative entitlements carry a recorded approval before they take effect. _(unmet → Block. This is the specific control every access-related audit tests first.)_
- **`acr.tenure_declared`** Every grant declares whether it is permanent, fixed-term, just-in-time or break-glass. _(unmet → Default to fixed_term with a short expiry rather than to permanent. Defaulting to permanent is the mechanical reason entitlement counts only ever rise.
)_
- **`acr.classification_known`** The sensitivity of what the entitlement reaches is recorded before it is granted. _(unmet → Treat as confidential and require review. Rule 10 cannot be enforced downstream on an entitlement whose reach is unclassified.
)_
- **`acr.revocation_path_known`** How this entitlement would be removed is known at the moment it is granted. _(unmet → Flag the grant. An entitlement nobody knows how to remove is a permanent one however it is labelled, and the discovery is always made on a leaver's last day.
)_


## Constraints

- **`acr.no_sod_pair`** An identity may not hold two entitlements a duty split forbids together.
- **`acr.no_shared_privileged_credential`** A privileged entitlement may not be held by a shared account.
- **`acr.special_category_needs_named_basis`** An entitlement reaching special-category personal data requires a recorded lawful basis and a named individual holder.
- **`acr.break_glass_time_bounded`** Break-glass access carries a mandatory expiry set at the moment it is granted.
- **`acr.no_revocation_without_evidence`** An entitlement may not be recorded as revoked without evidence from the target system.
- **`acr.review_by_someone_who_can_judge`** Recertification is performed by someone who knows what the holder does, not by whoever owns the system. _(soft)_
- **`acr.no_dormancy_sweep_without_usage_data`** Automated dormancy removal runs only where usage logging is available.


## Business rules

- **`acr.privileged_requires_mfa`** A privileged or administrative entitlement requires enrolled strong authentication.
- **`acr.leaver_revocation_is_immediate`** On confirmed departure every entitlement held by that identity moves to overdue at once, not at the next review.
- **`acr.mover_invalidates_review`** A role change invalidates every prior recertification for that identity.
- **`acr.no_permanent_contractor_access`** Contractor and vendor entitlements are fixed-term and expire with the engagement.
- **`acr.direct_grant_needs_justification`** A direct grant outside the role model carries a written justification and a shorter review interval.
- **`acr.orphan_cannot_be_recertified`** An orphaned entitlement cannot be recertified; it must be owned or removed.
- **`acr.never_used_after_ninety_days_is_removable`** An entitlement never exercised within ninety days of grant is proposed for removal by default.
- **`acr.account_disable_is_not_revocation`** Disabling the account does not close the revocation obligation for federated, physical or shared entitlements.


## Exceptions — where the rules above are legitimately wrong

- **Elevated access may be granted without prior approval during a declared incident, provided it carries an expiry set at grant time and is ratified within two working days.
** — A control that cannot be bypassed at three in the morning gets bypassed permanently instead of temporarily — the shared root credential appears and never leaves. The pre-set expiry is what keeps the exception an exception rather than a new default.
 _(overrides acr.approval_before_privileged_grant)_
- **Access existing solely for recovery or continuity is exempt from dormancy-based removal.** — Its value is precisely that it has never been needed. Sweeping it is the classic own goal: the quarterly job looks efficient right up to the quarter it matters.
 _(overrides acr.never_used_after_ninety_days_is_removable)_
- **Some supervised roles are required to hold specific access; it cannot be reduced on least-privilege grounds without breaching the regime that mandates it.
** — Least privilege is a principle, not a statute. Where a regulator mandates a capability, the correct response is a compensating control and a documented acceptance, not a removal.
 _(overrides acr.no_sod_pair)_
- **Below a headcount threshold a duty split may be impossible, and a compensating detective control replaces the preventive one.
** — In a ten-person company the same person raises and pays the invoice because there is nobody else. Pretending otherwise produces a policy everybody breaches daily, which is worse than a review control everybody follows.
 _(overrides acr.no_sod_pair)_
- **An identity serving notice retains access, under heightened monitoring, until the last working day.** — Revoking at resignation stops the handover that is the entire point of a notice period. The correct control is monitoring plus immediate removal of exfiltration-capable entitlements, not blanket removal.
 _(overrides acr.leaver_revocation_is_immediate)_
- **A registered service account may hold entitlements with no individual holder, provided a named owning team lead is recorded.** — The alternative is a fiction — assigning the account to whoever created it, who then leaves and orphans it. A named owner who inherits by role survives the departure.
 _(overrides acr.named_individual_holder)_


## Best practices

- **Capture a testable business reason at the moment of grant, in the requester's words, naming the work that cannot be done without it.** — It costs thirty seconds then and is unrecoverable later. Every organisation that cannot reduce access is one that did not do this, because review means testing the reason and there is nothing to test.

- **Default new grants to fixed-term with a short expiry, and require an argument for permanence.** — Reverses the ratchet. Permanent-by-default is the single mechanical cause of monotonically rising entitlement counts, and no amount of review effort compensates for it.

- **Run automated dormancy review before human recertification, and put only what survives in front of a person.** — Dormancy removes the uncontroversial third of the estate at no human cost and shortens the list a reviewer sees, which is the only variable that predicts whether they will actually look.

- **Review a whole identity's entitlements together, not one row at a time across many identities.** — Duty-split conflicts and privilege creep are properties of the set. Row-at-a-time review cannot see either, which is why organisations pass every recertification and still fail an SoD test.

- **Treat a role change as a full re-review of everything the identity holds, not as an additive provisioning event.** — Movers are where privilege accumulates. Joiners are provisioned because someone is waiting; leavers are deprovisioned because HR raises a ticket; movers just gain and never lose.

- **Close a revocation on evidence from the target system, never on a ticket status.** — Federated seats, API tokens, shared credentials and physical passes all survive account disablement, and every one of them has been produced as evidence of removal at some point.

- **Hold physical access in the same register as logical, or accept that leavers keep their pass.** — Facilities and IT run different systems with different leaver processes. The pass in the drawer is the most common unrevoked entitlement in any organisation with an office.

- **Every service account carries a named owning role, inherited on departure rather than attached to a person.** — Service accounts fail every control designed for people. Role-inherited ownership is the only one that survives the creator leaving.



## Anti-patterns

- **A quarterly review that retains almost everything it looks at, reported as a completed control.** — tempting because Reviewers are given long lists, no grant reasons and two buttons. Retaining is free and instant; revoking risks breaking someone's job and generating a complaint that lands on the reviewer. The incentives produce the observed outcome exactly.
 Instead: Measure removal rate rather than completion rate. Run dormancy first so the human list is short. Show the grant reason next to every row and let the reviewer see when it was last exercised.

- **Treating disablement of the primary account as the completion of the leaver process.** — tempting because It is one action, it is visible, it feels total, and the directory is the system everyone thinks of first. Everything else lives in a product nobody in IT administers.
 Instead: Enumerate the entitlement set per identity and close each one on system-side evidence. Track leaver_revocation_lag against the last entitlement closed, not the first.

- **Granting a role template and reporting it as least privilege because nobody got a direct grant.** — tempting because Roles are the efficient way to provision and the honest way to report. The template was sized for the most demanding member of the job family and is never resized downwards.
 Instead: Size templates to the median and handle the exceptions as short-lived direct grants. Compare template contents against actual usage per member annually.

- **"Give them the same access as Priya" as the provisioning instruction.** — tempting because It is fast, it is what the requester actually knows, and it works on day one. Nobody involved knows what Priya holds or why.
 Instead: Provision from a role template and require named additions with reasons. If cloning is unavoidable, clone and immediately schedule a thirty-day review of the copy.

- **Emergency access granted during an incident and still live months later.** — tempting because It is granted under maximum pressure and would have to be withdrawn under none. The incident closes, the ticket closes, and the withdrawal has no owner because the thing that justified it no longer exists to remind anyone.
 Instead: A mandatory expiry set at grant time, so closure requires nobody to remember.
- **An entitlement whose owner left, which nobody removes because nobody knows what depends on it.** — tempting because Removing it risks breaking something visible; leaving it risks nothing visible. The asymmetry is complete and it is the correct individual decision every single time.
 Instead: Time-box it: disable rather than delete, watch for breakage for a fixed period, then remove. Disablement makes the removal reversible, which is what makes the decision possible at all.

- **Running entitlement cleanup as a one-off remediation programme rather than as a standing process.** — tempting because An audit finding creates funding and a deadline. A project delivers a number, closes, and returns the team to their previous work.
 Instead: Fix the ratchet instead of the count: expire by default, require reasons at grant, and run dormancy continuously. The count then falls as a side effect and stays down.

## Inputs

- **portal** — the IAM platform's entitlement export — holder, permission, grant date, group membership
- **access_log** — whether the entitlement has actually been exercised, and when
- **hris** — employment state, start and end dates, manager, role changes
- **ticket** — the request and the stated business reason
- **signed_form** — acceptable-use and privileged-access acknowledgements
- **register** — the physical access register — passes, keys, floors
- **regulator** — the review obligation and its required interval
- **attestation** — the outcome of a recertification campaign
- **derived** — dormancy, orphan status and duty-split conflict computed across the identity's set


## Outputs

- **`removal_confidence_bp`** How safely this entitlement could be removed today. The number that turns access reduction from a negotiation into a queue.
 → L4.reasoning_unit, L4.decision_maker
- **`exposure_bp`** What is at stake if this identity is compromised. → L4.reasoning_unit
- **`review_debt_days`** How far past its own review obligation the organisation is on this row. → L4.reasoning_unit, L6.learning_unit
- **`revocation_path`** The ordered steps that would actually remove it — which is not "disable the account" for anything federated, physical or shared.
 → L5.execution_planning
- **`sod_conflict_set`**  → L4.reasoning_unit, L4.decision_maker
- **`notification_target`** Who should actually be told, which is the system owner far more often than the holder. → L5.2.channel_planner
- **`orphan_flag`**  → L4.reasoning_unit, L6.learning_unit


## Events

- **`acr.granted`** Access Granted
- **`acr.holder_moved`** Holder Changed Role — invalidates last_reviewed_at, review_outcome, grant_reason
- **`acr.leaver_detected`** Holder Left — invalidates holder_employment_state
- **`acr.review_completed`** Access Review Completed
- **`acr.revoked`** Access Revoked
- **`acr.became_orphaned`** Entitlement Orphaned
- **`acr.sod_conflict_detected`** Duty Split Breached
- **`acr.break_glass_opened`** Emergency Access Opened


## Actions

- **Grant the entitlement** (human) — Create the grant with a testable reason and a tenure. A grant recorded without both is a grant that can never be reviewed.

- **Revoke the entitlement** (human) — Remove it at the target system and capture evidence, not merely a ticket closure.
- **Reduce the entitlement** (human) — Replace an over-broad grant with a narrower one. Almost always the right outcome of a review and almost never the one recorded, because retain and revoke are the only buttons offered.

- **Recertify** (human) — Confirm the reason still holds. Irreversible in the sense that matters — the attestation becomes the evidence, and a careless one is worse than none because it stops the clock.

- **Find an owner for an orphaned entitlement** (human) — The only route out of `orphaned`, and expensive precisely because the cheap route — asking the person who created it — is gone.

- **Convert standing access to just-in-time** (human) — The largest available reduction in standing entitlement count. Unpopular because it moves cost from a column nobody measures into one everybody feels.

- **Escalate an unrevoked leaver entitlement** (human) —
- **Sweep dormant entitlements** (system) — Propose removal of everything unused past the threshold WHERE usage is observable. Running it over unobservable entitlements is how disaster-recovery access gets revoked the quarter before it is needed.

- **Withdraw emergency access** (human) —
- **Reconcile the record against the target system** (agent) — When the register and the system disagree, the system is right and the register is updated.


## Evidence

- **access_log** · 10000 bp — The target system's own record of what was exercised and when. Nothing outranks it, because it is the only source that observes behaviour rather than intent.

- **portal** · 9000 bp — The IAM platform export. Strong, and blind to everything federated or granted in a product's own admin UI.
- **signed_form** · 9000 bp — A privileged-access acknowledgement or acceptable-use form. Survives a dispute.
- **hris** · 8500 bp — Employment state. Authoritative for the leaver and mover triggers and for nothing else here.
- **regulator** · 9500 bp — The review obligation and its interval.
- **register** · 5000 bp — The physical access register. Usually a spreadsheet, usually stale, usually the only record of the pass in someone's drawer.
- **attestation** · 4500 bp — Deliberately ranked below the physical register. An attestation records a click, not a judgement, and a campaign that retains ninety-eight per cent of what it sees has produced almost no evidence about any individual row.

- **ticket** · 5500 bp — The request and its stated reason. Present far more often than it is testable.
- **derived** · 4000 bp — Dormancy, orphan status and duty-split conflict computed across the set. Corroborating only.


## Metrics

- **orphaned_entitlement_share** (percent) — Share of live entitlements with no resolvable owner. The headline number, and one almost nobody can produce.
- **leaver_revocation_lag** (hours) — Hours from confirmed departure to evidenced revocation. The number a regulator asks for, and the one that is measured in weeks wherever it has never been looked at.

- **dormant_entitlement_share** (percent) — Share unused in ninety days where usage is observable.
- **recertification_removal_rate** (percent) — Share of reviewed entitlements actually removed or reduced. A rate near zero does not mean the estate is clean; it means the review is not running, whatever the completion dashboard says.

- **grant_reason_completeness** (percent) — Share of live entitlements with a testable recorded reason. Bounds what any review can achieve.
- **privileged_entitlement_count** (count) —
- **sod_conflict_count** (count) —
- **revocation_evidence_rate** (percent) — Share of revocations proven at the target system rather than asserted in a ticket.

## Examples

- **Finance analyst who moved to Treasury** _(typical)_ — Kept ledger-posting rights, gained payment-release rights. Neither grant is wrong; together they are the textbook duty-split breach, and both passed their last recertification because each was reviewed on its own row.

- **Service account created for a 2019 migration** _(edge)_ — identity_type service_account, creator departed, privilege administrative, purpose unrecorded, last used unknown because logging was never enabled. Orphaned by every definition and untouched because nobody will risk the removal.

- **Building pass held by a leaver** _(typical)_ — Account disabled on the last working day, pass never collected, facilities register never reconciled against HRIS. Still opens the door eleven months later.

- **Break-glass root credential from a Sunday-night incident** _(edge)_ — Granted correctly and never withdrawn. Reviews as an exception, behaves as standing administrative access, and is held by whoever happened to be on call.

- **Contractor whose engagement ended** _(edge)_ — No HRIS leaver record because they were never an employee. The purchase order lapsed silently and the access did not. Contractors carry the leaver risk without the trigger that catches it.

- **Disaster-recovery access unused for four years** _(counterexample)_ — Reads as dormant on every metric and must never be swept. Its value is precisely that it has never been needed — the exemption exists for exactly this row.

- **Shared support mailbox credential** _(misclassification)_ — Routinely registered as one entitlement with one holder. It is one credential known to eleven people, unattributable and unrevocable without breaking a rota.

- **Read-only reporting access reaching salary data** _(misclassification)_ — Classified `internal` because it is read-only. `read` is an access_type, not a sensitivity — data_classification here is `personal` and the blast radius is organisation-wide.


## Metadata

owner **Admin** · updated 2026-08-08 · review **unreviewed** · confidence **provisional** · completeness **complete**


> Five of fourteen patterns are executable today and none of them is access-shaped — they run on generic thread, commitment and graph-degree primitives, which is the honest state of play rather than a gap in authoring. The ranked Layer 1/2 ask this object generates is: (1) access.last_used_at, the single highest-value signal in the Admin brain, because it converts access reduction from a negotiation into an observation; (2) leaver_confirmed, shared with employee_record and asset — one event, three objects, and the highest-consequence gap in the domain; (3) access.reviewed_at plus access.granted_at, without which no review clock can start; (4) derived.entitlement_set_by_identity, because duty-split conflict is a property of the set and no per-row review can ever see it; (5) sod.conflict_pairs, which already exists as an internal-audit spreadsheet connected to nothing. Authored as the third of the custody trio with admin.obj.core.asset and admin.obj.core.employee_record — the three share one failure shape (the grant nobody removed when the reason ended) and one missing event.
